newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt criticises Israel before economic meeting.
newsitem.headline: Egypt criticises Israel before economic meeting.

text.p: Egypt called on Saturday for Israel to ease its tough line in peace talks, days before the convening of a Middle East and North Africa economic conference grouping Israel and Arab countries.
"We are not going to wait forever until (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu changes his horse," Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said.
Moussa said the formula of "peace for land" agreed in Madrid in 1991 but now rejected by Netanyahu, is the only way towards a comprehensive settlement in the region.
"Flouting with the rules (set by) the Madrid conference, the U.N., and the Oslo agreement, should not reward Israel at all," he added
Moussa responded tersely when asked why Cairo is hosting the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) conference despite the impasse in peace talks.

"The region should not be held hostage to Israeli policies," he told the Foreign Press Association in advance of Tuesday's opening of the conference. "We are going ahead with our plans regardless of what the Israelis say or do."
The annual conference is the third aimed at integrating the region's economy. But some Arab states, angered at Israeli policies, have questioned holding the meeting before full Arab-Israel peace.
Moussa expressed the hope Israel would get the message that "playing havoc with the peace process is not permitted."
Israel and the PLO are currently locked in U.S.-brokered negotiations on implementing a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Moussa predicted the United States would play a more active role in the region after this week's re-election of President Bill Clinton, but encouraged European participation.

"We all expect more activities by the new Clinton administration. We have always expressed the view that we believe in the necessity in continuing an American role as an honest broker between the Arabs and Israel.
"But...the European role is major and important," he added, "particularly, in the light of Israeli stubborness, which has not been affected enough by the existing roles."
